lessonTitle: DNA Structure and Replication: The Antiparallel Helix, the Replication Fork and Okazaki Fragments

blocks.text: Before a cell divides it copies about six billion base pairs of DNA in a matter of hours, with an error rate of roughly one in a billion. A bacterial infection can be treated by blocking one enzyme of this process, and a herpesvirus drug works by sneaking a fake building block into the new strand. To see why, you need to see how the double helix is built and how it is copied.

blocks.markdown: **DNA is a polymer of nucleotides.** Each nucleotide has a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group and one of four nitrogenous bases: the purines **adenine (A)** and **guanine (G)** and the pyrimidines **cytosine (C)** and **thymine (T)**. Nucleotides are joined by **phosphodiester bonds** between the 3' hydroxyl of one sugar and the 5' phosphate of the next, giving a sugar-phosphate backbone with a direction: one end has a free 5' phosphate (the 5' end) and the other a free 3' hydroxyl (the 3' end). Numbers with a prime refer to the carbons of deoxyribose.

blocks.title: Antiparallel double helix and base pairing
blocks.text: A DNA molecule consists of two polynucleotide strands wound around each other in a right-handed double helix. The strands are antiparallel: one runs 5' to 3' while its partner runs 3' to 5'. The bases lie inside the helix and pair by hydrogen bonds: A pairs with T (two hydrogen bonds) and G pairs with C (three hydrogen bonds). The two strands are therefore complementary, and the sequence of one strand specifies the other.

blocks.markdown: **Quantitative features.** The helix has a diameter of about 2 nm, a rise of about 0.34 nm per base pair, and about 10 base pairs per full turn (so about 3.4 nm per turn). The helix has a wide **major groove** and a narrower **minor groove**, where regulatory proteins can read the base sequence. **Chargaff's rules** follow from base pairing: in double-stranded DNA the amount of A equals T and the amount of G equals C, so purines equal pyrimidines (A + G = T + C). Because G-C pairs have three hydrogen bonds, DNA with a high G + C content is more stable and melts at a higher temperature.

blocks.title: Using Chargaff's rules and helix geometry
blocks.prompt: A sample of double-stranded DNA is 1020 base pairs long and contains 18% thymine. Calculate (a) the percentage of cytosine, and (b) the length of the molecule in nanometres, using 0.34 nm per base pair.

steps.text: A = T, so adenine is also 18%. A + T = 36%.
The rest is G + C = 100 - 36 = 64%. Since G = C, each is half of this.
Length equals the number of base pairs times the rise per base pair.

blocks.answer: (a) Cytosine is 32%; (b) the molecule is about 347 nm long (about 102 turns of the helix).

blocks.markdown: **Replication is semiconservative.** The Meselson-Stahl experiment showed that each daughter molecule contains one original (parental) strand and one newly synthesised strand. Replication starts at specific sequences called **origins of replication**. Bacteria have one origin on their circular chromosome, whereas each human chromosome has many origins, so that the large genome is copied quickly. From each origin, two **replication forks** move away in opposite directions (bidirectional replication), creating a replication bubble.

rows: Unwinds the double helix by breaking hydrogen bonds between base pairs, using ATP
Coat the separated single strands and stop them re-annealing
Cuts and reseals DNA to relieve the supercoiling ahead of the fork (bacterial DNA gyrase is a target of quinolone antibiotics)
A specialised RNA polymerase that synthesises a short RNA primer, providing a free 3' hydroxyl
Extends the primer by adding nucleotides in the 5' to 3' direction, using the template strand; proofreads with 3' to 5' exonuclease activity
Removes RNA primers and replaces them with DNA
Joins adjacent DNA fragments by forming the final phosphodiester bond
blocks.caption: Enzymes of the replication fork.

blocks.markdown: **Why DNA polymerase needs a primer and works only 5' to 3'.** DNA polymerase adds each new nucleotide to the free **3' hydroxyl** group at the end of an existing strand: the incoming nucleotide triphosphate supplies the energy by releasing pyrophosphate. Polymerase cannot start a chain from nothing, so primase first makes an RNA primer. Because it can only extend a 3' end, synthesis always proceeds in the 5' to 3' direction. This simple rule underlies the fork's asymmetry. Drugs exploit it: dideoxynucleotides and acyclovir-type nucleoside analogues lack the 3' hydroxyl, so once incorporated they terminate chain elongation.

blocks.title: Leading and lagging strands
blocks.text: The two parental strands are antiparallel, but polymerase only moves 5' to 3'. At each fork the leading strand is template for continuous synthesis in the same direction as the fork moves (needing one primer). The lagging strand is synthesised discontinuously, away from the fork, in short Okazaki fragments, each needing its own RNA primer. The primers are then removed, the gaps filled with DNA and the fragments joined by ligase.

blocks.markdown: **Okazaki fragments explained.** The helicase opens the helix in one direction. On the strand whose 3' end faces the fork, polymerase can follow the helicase continuously (leading strand). On the other template, new DNA would have to be made in the direction *toward* the fork's movement, which means making it 3' to 5', and polymerase cannot do this. The cell solves the problem by letting the opening fork expose a stretch of template, laying down a primer, synthesising a short piece back toward the previous primer, and repeating. Fragments are about 1000-2000 nucleotides long in bacteria and about 100-200 nucleotides in eukaryotes.

blocks.title: How long does it take to copy a bacterial chromosome?
blocks.prompt: A circular bacterial chromosome of 3.0 million base pairs has a single origin, with two forks moving in opposite directions, each at 800 nucleotides per second. How long does replication take, and how many Okazaki fragments would be made on one lagging-strand arm of 1.5 million nucleotides if each fragment is 1500 nucleotides?

steps.text: Two forks share the chromosome, so the combined speed is 2 x 800 = 1600 nucleotides per second.
Time equals genome size divided by the combined speed.
One arm of the lagging template of 1.5 million nucleotides gives this many fragments.

blocks.answer: About 31 minutes, with about 1000 Okazaki fragments on that lagging-strand arm.

items: Helicase unwinds the helix at the replication fork; single-strand binding proteins stabilise the strands.
Primase lays down an RNA primer on each template.
DNA polymerase extends each primer 5' to 3'; continuous on the leading strand, discontinuous on the lagging strand.
Primers are removed and replaced by DNA.
Ligase seals the nicks between fragments.

blocks.title: Direction of reading versus direction of synthesis
blocks.text: The template strand is read 3' to 5' while the new strand is built 5' to 3'. Many errors in exams come from mixing these up. Remember that polymerase adds nucleotides to a 3' hydroxyl, never to a 5' end.

points: DNA is an antiparallel, right-handed double helix of two complementary strands: A pairs with T by two hydrogen bonds and G with C by three.
Replication is semiconservative and bidirectional; helicase, single-strand binding proteins, primase, DNA polymerase and ligase act at each fork.
DNA polymerase needs a 3' hydroxyl and synthesises only 5' to 3', so the lagging strand is made in short Okazaki fragments that are later joined by ligase.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the two strands of the DNA double helix?

options.text: They run in opposite directions and are held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases
They run in the same direction and are held together by phosphodiester bonds between bases
They run in opposite directions and are held together by ionic bonds between phosphates
They run in the same direction and pair purine with purine

questions.correctOptionText: They run in opposite directions and are held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases

distractorRationale.a: Correct: antiparallel strands with hydrogen-bonded complementary pairing.
distractorRationale.b: Strands are antiparallel, and phosphodiester bonds link nucleotides within one strand, not across strands.
distractorRationale.c: Phosphates lie on the outside backbone; the strands are held by base-pair hydrogen bonds.
distractorRationale.d: Pairing is always purine with pyrimidine, and the strands are antiparallel.

questions.explanation: The two strands are antiparallel, with one running 5' to 3' and the other 3' to 5'. Complementary pairs (A-T and G-C) are joined by hydrogen bonds, while phosphodiester bonds form the backbone of each strand.

questions.stem: Which enzyme provides the free 3' hydroxyl group that DNA polymerase needs to begin synthesis at the replication fork?

options.text: Primase, by making a short RNA primer

questions.correctOptionText: Primase, by making a short RNA primer

distractorRationale.a: Correct: primase synthesises an RNA primer whose 3' hydroxyl DNA polymerase can extend.
distractorRationale.b: Helicase opens the helix but does not create a primer.
distractorRationale.c: Ligase seals nicks after polymerisation; it does not start chains.
distractorRationale.d: Topoisomerase relieves supercoiling ahead of the fork.

questions.explanation: DNA polymerase cannot start a strand de novo, only add nucleotides to an existing 3' hydroxyl. Primase is an RNA polymerase that lays down a short RNA primer, giving polymerase a starting point.

questions.stem: A student claims that both new strands at a replication fork are made continuously. What is the main reason this is incorrect?

options.text: Polymerase synthesises only 5' to 3', so the strand whose synthesis must run away from the fork is made in short fragments
Helicase can only open the helix on one parental strand
Ligase is missing from the lagging strand
Primase works only on the leading strand

questions.correctOptionText: Polymerase synthesises only 5' to 3', so the strand whose synthesis must run away from the fork is made in short fragments

distractorRationale.a: Correct: antiparallel templates plus unidirectional polymerase require discontinuous synthesis on one strand.
distractorRationale.c: Ligase is needed on the lagging strand to join fragments.
distractorRationale.d: Primase acts repeatedly on the lagging strand, once for each fragment.

questions.explanation: Because the template strands are antiparallel and polymerase works only in the 5' to 3' direction, one strand is made continuously (leading) while the other is made in short Okazaki fragments, each starting with an RNA primer, and later joined by ligase.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a feature of semiconservative replication?

options.text: Each daughter double helix contains one parental strand and one newly synthesised strand
One daughter helix has both parental strands and the other has both new strands
Each daughter helix is a random mixture of parental and new fragments
Both daughter helices contain only new DNA

questions.correctOptionText: Each daughter double helix contains one parental strand and one newly synthesised strand

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this is the semiconservative model shown by Meselson and Stahl.
distractorRationale.b: This is the conservative model, which was rejected.
distractorRationale.c: This is the dispersive model, not supported by the evidence.
distractorRationale.d: This is not a model of replication; parental information would be lost.

questions.explanation: In semiconservative replication each parental strand serves as a template for a new complementary strand, so every daughter molecule is a hybrid of one old and one new strand. Meselson and Stahl's density experiment supported this.

questions.stem: A double-stranded DNA sample contains 21% adenine. What percentage of the bases is guanine? Give your answer in percent (%).
questions.explanation: By Chargaff's rules A = T, so T is also 21% and A + T is 42%. That leaves 58% for G + C, and since G = C each is 29%.

questions.stem: A circular bacterial chromosome of 4.8 million base pairs is replicated from a single origin by two forks moving in opposite directions, each at 1000 nucleotides per second. How long does replication take, in minutes?
questions.explanation: Two forks together copy 2000 nucleotides per second, so the time is 4.8 x 10^6 / 2000 = 2400 s. Dividing by 60 s per minute gives 40 minutes.

questions.stem: True or false: DNA polymerase can add a nucleotide to the 5' end of a growing strand.
questions.explanation: DNA polymerase adds nucleotides only to the 3' hydroxyl of an existing strand, so synthesis proceeds 5' to 3'. This restriction is the reason the lagging strand is made as Okazaki fragments.

questions.stem: Describe the antiparallel double helix and explain how base-pairing rules lead to Chargaff's rules and to the idea that one strand specifies the other.
markingGuide: Two polynucleotide strands with sugar-phosphate backbones joined by 3'-5' phosphodiester bonds; strands run in opposite (antiparallel) directions.
Bases face inwards; purine pairs with pyrimidine: A-T (two hydrogen bonds), G-C (three hydrogen bonds).
Right-handed helix with about 10 base pairs per turn, major and minor grooves.
Chargaff's rules: A = T and G = C, purines equal pyrimidines in double-stranded DNA.
Complementarity means the sequence of one strand determines the other, enabling accurate copying.
questions.explanation: Specific pairing means that each base on one strand has a unique partner on the other, so equal amounts of A and T, G and C result and either strand can act as a template for the other.

questions.stem: Outline the roles of helicase, primase, DNA polymerase and DNA ligase in replicating a leading and a lagging strand.
markingGuide: Helicase unwinds the double helix at the fork; single-strand binding proteins stabilise the strands and topoisomerase relieves supercoiling.
Primase makes short RNA primers (one on the leading strand, many on the lagging).
DNA polymerase extends primers 5' to 3'; leading strand continuously, lagging strand as Okazaki fragments; also proofreads.
Primers are removed and replaced with DNA.
DNA ligase seals the nicks between Okazaki fragments to give a continuous strand.
questions.explanation: The enzymes act in sequence: unwinding, priming, extending and finally joining, with the leading strand needing only one primer and the lagging strand needing many.

questions.stem: Explain why the lagging strand is synthesised as Okazaki fragments, and why a nucleoside analogue lacking a 3' hydroxyl group acts as a chain terminator.
markingGuide: The two template strands are antiparallel but DNA polymerase synthesises only 5' to 3' by adding to a 3' hydroxyl.
One template (leading) allows continuous synthesis in the direction of fork movement.
On the other template synthesis must run away from the fork, so short fragments (Okazaki fragments) are made, each needing an RNA primer.
Primers are removed, gaps filled and fragments joined by ligase.
An analogue lacking the 3' hydroxyl can be incorporated but the next nucleotide cannot be attached, so chain elongation stops.
questions.explanation: Polymerase directionality forces discontinuous synthesis on one strand. The same requirement for a 3' hydroxyl explains why analogues lacking it terminate synthesis.
